sentences.sentence: On an edge GPU, most of a VLA's action chunk goes to vision, so a method that speeds up or smooths chunking keeps only the part of its benefit that touches the seam between chunks.
We re-measured seven training-free methods, published with desktop-GPU numbers, where a low-cost robot runs its policy: SmolVLA on a Jetson Orin NX.
Every gate had its threshold committed before the run, and all of them share one checkpoint and the same recorded episodes, so every number traces to a result file and a protocol commit.
The vision encoder alone takes 151.0 of 219.0 ms of server time per chunk (25 W).
The two seam methods pass: a gradient-free prefix overwrite cuts the boundary jump by 72 % or more, and movement-primitive seam conditioning removes most of the seam jerk.
Sampling does not transfer, because on a sequential edge engine every N-sample method pays for N chunks in series.
So on this board, smooth the seam and leave the sampler alone.
With several training-free chunking tricks published this year for flow-matching VLAs, it is tempting to think they make a policy faster or smoother on any robot.
Their numbers come from desktop and data-centre GPUs (RTX 4090, A100, H100, RTX 5090).
There a chunk costs tens of milliseconds, and spare compute can hide an extra pass.
A robot people can buy runs its policy on an edge GPU instead, where most of the chunk goes to a part the tricks never touch (the vision encoder).
So the useful question is how much of each trick is left on that board.
Ours is an SO-101 arm [arXiv:2606.08881] with a Jetson Orin NX 16 GB, running SmolVLA [arXiv:2506.01844] through vla.cpp, a C++ inference engine, on episodes recorded with LeRobot.
This paper started once SmolVLA ran on the arm through vla.cpp: the next question was where the remaining time of a chunk went, and which published tricks could still buy something.
We took seven of them.
Each answer is a gate with a bar committed before the number; offline effects get an episode bootstrap, and latencies are medians of at least 50 calls.
The appendix maps every number to its result file and protocol commit.
Follow one chunk.
At ten Euler steps and full power (MAXN_SUPER) it costs 237.5 ms end to end: 150.7 ms of vision, 14.9 ms of prefill and 5.3 ms per denoise step (Fig. 1).
At 25 W the server-side split is 151.0 ms of vision in 219.0 ms.
A trick that only touches the denoising loop therefore works on at most a quarter of that chunk.
Two power modes appear because each gate's protocol froze the mode it ran in (the serving split and the boundary experiments at 25 W, the latency experiments at full power).
Every number below carries its mode.
All offline effects use the same SmolVLA checkpoint and the same 20 recorded episodes, with 254 chunk boundaries per delay.
Table 1 carries every effect, bar and verdict; the text covers what the table cannot show.
The two tricks that pass both act where our chunk meets the next one.
Overwriting the new chunk's executed prefix with the actions already committed passes the 50 % jump-cut bar at every delay, in PyTorch and in vla.cpp, where it adds 0.4 ms per chunk.
Movement-primitive chunking [arXiv:2610.39451] passes as well.

Projecting each chunk onto ten Gaussian bases keeps the error within its bar while removing within-chunk jerk, and conditioning on the last action sent removes 83–87 % of the seam jerk at +0.19° of error (its paper reports 73–84 %; ours is measured on the commanded stream only).
Exact real-time chunking [arXiv:2506.07339], which inpaints the prefix with guidance instead of overwriting it, cuts the jump by less than the 50 % pass mark at every delay (Fig. 2).
It also costs 1.9× a naive chunk in PyTorch.
Cutting the Euler steps from ten to two [arXiv:2610.32102] saves 41 ms per chunk at full power (real, but small next to the vision cost).

The paper's central claim, that the action cloud contracts around an unchanged centroid, is not proven here: our cloud ratio of 0.78 falls between the bar of 0.70 and the fail line of 0.85, where the paper reports 0.51 on π0.
The paper also expects fewer steps to remove edge-GPU thermal throttling, but our Orin did not throttle at ten steps in either power mode.
We keep ten steps, as the protocol's rule says while the contraction is unproven.
Both sampling tricks pay for their samples one after another.

Speculative chunk selection [arXiv:2610.28019] uses the pre-commit frame to pick, among four candidates, the chunk closest to the recorded teleoperation continuation, and offline it does beat a random pick (one continuation per frame, training-set episodes, open loop).
Its paper promises no added control-step delay.
On the Orin, vla.cpp samples the candidates in sequence, so a cycle costs 1,200 ms and 37 control ticks against 8 for a naive chunk (Fig. 3).
Entropy-adaptive chunk length [arXiv:2604.04161] is the clearest miss.
One 20-sample decision takes 4,751 ms on the Orin against a threshold of 298 ms, because the samples run one after another.
Its chosen length also sits at the floor in both task phases, and the jump is no better than with fixed chunks and the overwrite.
Turn on the prefix overwrite and the primitive projection with seam conditioning.
Both act on the seam, which the vision cost does not hide, and each costs under a millisecond on this board, so there is little reason to leave them off.
Ten Euler steps stay until the contraction passes its threshold; the two-step saving is real but small because vision dominates.
Sampling several chunks per decision does not pay on a sequential edge engine, since exact guidance, speculative selection and adaptive length all pay for N chunks in series.
Before turning one of them on, check whether your engine samples in a batch (ours does not).
This version is offline and latency only.
The closed-loop columns on the arm, seam smoothing and the overwrite in the robot client, belong to a longer version.

Other chunking tricks are also reported on desktop-class GPUs, and we did not re-measure them here: extending the executing chunk instead of resampling [arXiv:2610.05719], reactive chunking driven by a latent world model [arXiv:2606.18589], and fine-tuning the policy for latency with reinforcement learning [arXiv:2608.23831].
On the engine side, TurboVLA [arXiv:2607.27205] pushes VLA throughput on a desktop GPU, while vla.cpp, the engine we measure, runs VLAs on edge boards.
Two works use the same arm.
A standardized benchmark reports failures and recoveries of VLA policies [arXiv:2606.08881], and a fleet of SO-101 cells evaluates policies at scale [arXiv:2607.24481].
Both evaluate policies, while we re-measure the execution tricks around one policy under bars fixed before the run.
The sampling result is conditional on the engine. vla.cpp samples sequentially, and we contribute to it (the overwrite runs on our fork, X).
Parity and determinism checks against PyTorch on the same board are in the gate logs.
A batched sampler is the control that would test the conclusion, and it has not run.
Effects other than latency are offline, measured on 20 recorded demonstrations of one task family (bowls) that the policy was trained on.

The arm gates for seam smoothing and for the overwrite in the robot client are the next step; the adaptive-length arm gate was left out because SmolVLA is at ceiling on this task, so a gain could not show.
Latency rows run at MAXN_SUPER and the serving and boundary rows at 25 W, which makes power mode a confound wherever the two are compared.
The study covers one policy, SmolVLA at 450M, since π0-class models do not fit on the Orin.

sentences.sentence: Every number in this paper is recomputable from the repository; this table maps each experiment to its files.
Fig. 1 — where one SmolVLA chunk's time goes on the Orin NX (vla.cpp, ten Euler steps, MAXN_SUPER): vision is most of it
Table 1: Seven tricks on one checkpoint.
Read the acts-on column against the verdict: the seam tricks pass, the sampling tricks fail.
Fig. 2 — median boundary-jump cut against naive asynchronous execution (254 boundaries per delay, 25 W): the overwrite clears the 50 % bar at every delay, exact RTC guidance does not.
Fig. 3 — cost per decision on the Orin NX (log scale, MAXN_SUPER): both sampling methods miss their bar (dashed: AAC's 298 ms; PACT's bar is one chunk, 237.5 ms).
